title: Economic torts protect against certain intentional interference with contracts, trade or business

content.overview: Economic torts protect against certain intentional interference with contracts, trade or business. The law does not create a general right to be free from competition.
content.glance: Economic torts protect against certain intentional interference with contracts, trade or business. The law does not create a general right to be free from competition.
content.study: Economic torts protect against certain intentional interference with contracts, trade or business. The law does not create a general right to be free from competition.\n\nLumley v Gye recognised intentional procurement of breach of contract. Mogul Steamship shows that lawful competition causing loss is not itself tortious. The exact economic tort and required intent must be identified.

sections.heading: Provenance, Legislative Objective & Doctrinal Foundations
sections.body: Lumley v Gye recognised intentional procurement of breach of contract. Mogul Steamship shows that lawful competition causing loss is not itself tortious. The exact economic tort and required intent must be identified.

sections.heading: Textual Anatomy, Provisos & Statutory Deconstruction
sections.body: The field is common-law and overlaps with contract and competition law. Liability depends on a recognised interference and the required unlawful means or intention.

sections.heading: Mandatory Proving Ingredients & Essential Elements
sections.body: 1. Identify the protected contractual or business interest. 2. Identify defendant conduct. 3. Prove required intent and unlawful means. 4. Prove causation and economic loss.

sections.heading: Evidentiary Burdens under BSA 2023 (ss. 104–106 & s. 63)
sections.body: Contracts, correspondence, market data and transaction records are central. The causal link between interference and loss must be proved.

sections.heading: Procedural Roadmap, Competent Forum & Limitation Act Checkpoints
sections.body: Civil court jurisdiction ordinarily applies, subject to competition-law or statutory regimes. Limitation depends on the cause.

examples.title: Illustration 1 — Doctrine Satisfied
examples.body: Intentional procurement of breach may be actionable, while lawful competition causing loss is not by itself a tort.

examples.title: Illustration 2 — Boundary Defect
examples.body: Economic loss must flow from a recognised actionable interference.

distinctions.title: Interference with contract vs lawful competition
distinctions.right: Contractual interference requires a recognised tort and intent; competition may lawfully divert customers.

rows.left: Intentional procurement of breach may be actionable, while lawful competition causing loss is not by itself a tort.
rows.right: Contractual interference requires a recognised tort and intent; competition may lawfully divert customers.

rows.left: Apply the ingredients of the pleaded tort.
rows.right: Do not substitute the neighbouring cause of action.

misconceptions.trap: Economic loss automatically proves a tort
misconceptions.correction: Economic loss must flow from a recognised actionable interference.
